## Discussion

This study shows a complex epidemic scenario amongst treatment-naïve HIV-1 infected children from the Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region, which seems to have persisted for more than a decade, between 2001 and 2012. We observed the co-circulation of pure HIV-1 subtypes and diverse and rare recombinant forms, including CRF02_AG and CRF45_cpx, coupled with a reduction in the prevalence of TDRM from 2001–2007 to the 2008–2012 period.

HIV infection in children is challenging, mainly due to the immaturity status of the immune response [43]. Disease progression in vertically infected children shows mainly two key distinct patterns: early progression, with the median age of symptom onset at 4 months of age; or late progression, with a median age of symptom onset at 6 years old [43–45]. A meta-analysis evaluating CD4+ T cells levels and viral load in children as predictors of disease progression [46] found that children older than two years old had an increased risk of progression to AIDS when the CD4+ T cell percentages were below 15% and when the viral load exceeded 105 copies per mL [46]. In our study, regardless of the period analyzed, most individuals had CD4+ T cell levels above 500 cells/mm3, with a gradual decrease observed in the older groups. This was expected since the number of CD4 cells in children gradually decrease with age progression until approach to adult values [47]. Until 2007, the viral load levels were slightly lower than those observed in the 2008–2012 period, with median viral loads reaching the highest levels (105 viral copies per mL) in children under five years. According to the PENTA guidelines [48], ART should be started urgently in all infants irrespective of clinical or immunological stage. In children aged > 12 months with no or minor symptoms (CDC clinical stage A or N or WHO stage 1 or 2), ART should be started when the CD4+ T cell count falls below 1000 cells/mm3 for children aged 3 to 3 for children aged 1 to 3 years or when the CD4+ T cell count falls below 500 cells/mm 5 years. In children >5 years, the treatment should start when the CD4+ T cell count falls below 350 cells/mm3.

In 2011, the World Health Organization defined criteria for the Global Plan and eliminate pediatric HIV infections in the world by 2015 [49]. The proposed targets range from the completion of at least one prenatal consultation and an HIV diagnosis for 95% of pregnant women during prenatal care and the immediate initiation of antiretroviral therapy for 90% of HIV-infected pregnant women. The Brazilian government acts actively to reduce the HIV-1 vertical transmission by offering free prenatal and delivery coverage, as well as ensuring universal and free access to ART, HIV follow-up screenings, and breastmilk substitutes. Therefore, the follow-up of the antiretroviral naïve pediatric population tends to become increasingly rare. The presence of ARV-resistant HIV strains in untreated individuals may occur in the setting of broad ARV coverage due to factors such as poor adherence to treatment regimens, combined with the lower genetic barrier of some drugs [50]. These variants that carry antiretroviral resistance mutations may limit the future availability of therapeutic options in newly infected individuals, especially in children who acquired the infection perinatally, increasing the risk of virological failure.

In this study, we found different scenarios regarding the TDRM prevalence in the two time periods analyzed: in the 2001–2007 period, the overall TDRM prevalence was high (24%), reducing to moderate levels (10%) in the 2008–2012 period. The TDRM reported in the Brazilian pediatric population is historically low, ranging from 0% to 12.8% [13,18–20,51]. One study from Manaus—Brazil, on the other hand, reported a TDRM prevalence of 16.2% in children, indicating that the TDRM prevalence scenario in Brazil may be more complex than previously thought [17]. The high TDRM prevalence found in this study in the 2001–2007 period could be partially explained by the therapy adopted in Brazil until 2007 to prevent MTCT. The preventive MTCT standard of care was initially based on the monotherapy with zidovudine, which was later modified to a dual-therapy regimen based on transcriptase inhibitors [12,52]. TDRM conferring resistance to AZT (M41L, F77L, T215I/Y/E/D) were found in 13% of the individuals assessed in 2001–2007, decreasing to 4% in the 2008–2012 sampling period. The zidovudine monotherapy for HIV-1 MTCT prevention can lead to a selection of minority resistant HIV-1 populations that can be transmitted during childbirth [53]. Furthermore, zidovudine monotherapy and a higher maternal viral load were already described as significantly associated with transmission [4]. The moderate TDRM levels observed in this pediatric population since 2008 reflect the advantages of adopting triple antiretroviral therapy, comprising two NRTIs and one NRTI as the initial regimen for children [12]. The moderate TDRM found was lower than a study conducted in Rio de Janeiro including ART-naïve patients with acute/recent HIV infection that found an overall TDRM prevalence of 16.3% [21].

A previous study associated the presence of any DRM in the mother with the presence of any DRMs in infants, supporting the recommendation that all pregnant women and HIV-infected infants undergo HIV genotypic resistance testing prior to initiation of ART [54]. In our study, regardless of the period evaluated, 19 children (14%) had some TDRM. Of these, 89% had viral strains resistant to reverse transcriptase inhibitor drugs, with 53% conferring mutations exclusively for NRTI, 21% only for NNRTI, and 16% for both. Contrasting with our results, in a study conducted on newly diagnosed untreated HIV-infected children from Rio de Janeiro sampled between 2000 and 2003, no TDRM was found. The authors suggested that as most of the children were the index case in the family, the perinatal transmission likely occurred from individuals not aware of their HIV status, and then, no prophylaxis therapy was adopted [20]. Only two individuals had TDRM for NNRTI+PI and PI. Both the M184V and the T215I mutations were the most frequent for the NRTI class. M184V is selected in therapeutic regimens that include the antiretroviral drugs 3TC/FCT and reduces susceptibility to these by up to 100-fold [55]. Furthermore, it gives a low level of resistance to ABC, while it increases susceptibility to drugs such as AZT and TDF [34]. T215I is a thymidine analog mutation (TAM) that may confer a low level of resistance to AZT [55]. For the NNRTI class, the most frequent mutation was K103N, which is known to be selected in individuals who received treatment with NVP or EFV [34]. This mutation confers high resistance to these two drugs. The prevalence of TDRM against NNRTI class, mainly K103N mutation, still poses an important threat to the ART response (virologic clearance) in the HIV-1-infected population from Rio de Janeiro in recent times [21].

The historical context is important to understanding the dynamics of the molecular diversity changing in the HIV-1 epidemics. In Brazil, several studies reported HIV-1 epidemics dominated by subtypes B, F1, C, and the recombinants among them, with a recent trend in the increase of diversity [28,29]. In this context, our study represents an important background to understanding the HIV-1 diversity of the Rio de Janeiro state in the heterosexual population, since the vertically infected children represent a proxy of the heterosexual route of transmission. Contrary to expected, there was no significant difference in HIV-1 diversity between the two periods, indicating that the HIV epidemic profile in the pediatric population of Rio de Janeiro exhibits a remarkable prevalence of non-B subtypes and recombinant forms since the beginning of the 2000s. It is important to note that the finding observed here likely reflect transmission events occurring years before sampling, since the children in our pediatric cohort were born between 1993 and 2012, and probably got infected via MTCT. In this regard, previous studies conducted with pregnant women in Rio de Janeiro found a significant increase in the HIV-1 non-B clades from 2005 to 2015 [25,26], and our results indicate that the change in the subtype B prevalence in Rio de Janeiro probably started several years before.

All subtype B sequences identified in this study clustered within the BPANDEMIC clade, confirming that this clade accounts for almost all subtype B infections in the Rio de Janeiro state [56]. The absence of subtype C in the 2001–2007 period and its low prevalence in the 2008–2012 period indicates that the sampling period is prior to the influx of this clade from the Brazilian southern region [57]. Some unique recombinant forms found in this study showed similar mosaic structures to other sequences from Brazil. Two putative new CRFs carrying the subtypes B and F1 were found, comprising isolates from Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo states. More studies are necessary to determine whether these recombinant sequences represent new CRFs or are simply URF displaying the same recombination pattern in the pol region. Besides the HIV-1 pure subtypes and CRFs classically found in the HIV-1 epidemic in Brazil [29], we also found one CRF02_AG and four CRF45_cpx sequences. The CRF02_AG strain branched within a cluster that has spread locally in Rio de Janeiro state over the last 30 years [31,57]. The four CRF45_cpx strains identified in this study were previously described as participating in an autochthonous transmission network that has spread to the Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, and Minas Gerais states [32]. The high molecular diversity found in the HIV-1-infected pediatric population indicates that the Rio de Janeiro state has acted as a hub for the introduction and spread of new HIV-1 clades in the Brazilian HIV epidemic since the 2000s.

The main limitation of this study was the distinct age of the populations sampled in the two periods. These differences could introduce a bias since some TDRM could revert in older prenatally ART-naïve infected children [58], resulting in an underestimation of their prevalence. It is important to point out that all children included in this study were ART drug-naïve at the moment of inclusion and the majority (65%) of the children included in the 2008–2012 period were <5 years. The prevalence of TDRM was similar in the overall sample of the 2008–2012 period (10/97) compared with the subsample (6/63) of children <5 years (10% versus 9.5%, respectively). However, caution is warranted when comparing this study with others since it represents an epidemiological scenario from more than ten years ago. In that period, the universal access to ART began to be expanded in Brazil, with the offer of new pediatric therapeutic options that facilitated the initiation of global goals for the end of the AIDS epidemic by 2030 (90-90-90) established in 2014 by UNAIDS.

# Conclusions

In summary, the results presented here indicate an important decrease in the TDRM prevalence in the pediatric population in Rio de Janeiro between 2001–2007 and 2008–2012 while no differences were observed in the HIV-1 molecular diversity among these two periods. The TDRM found may limit the future therapeutic options in the children infected perinatally, increasing the risk of virological failure. Our study also found high molecular diversity circulating in Rio de Janeiro since the beginning of the 2000s, with the presence of HIV-1 clades rarely detected in Brazil. More studies are necessary to evaluate the TDR prevalence in HIV-infected children in more recent periods, especially considering pretreatment genotyping assessment to determine the optimal ART regimen to be used.

# Targeting HIV Prevention Based on Molecular Epidemiology Among Deeply Sampled Subnetworks of Men Who Have Sex With Men

As the number of people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
in China approaches 1 million, with a national prevalence of 0.06% \[ 1
\], it is imperative to understand how the HIV epidemic in China is
spreading. The latest surveillance efforts estimate that almost half of
prevalent HIV infections in China were contracted through heterosexual
contact, almost a third were contracted through exposures during
injection drug use, and around 17% were contracted through male
homosexual exposures \[ 1 \]. The proportion of new infections among men
who have sex with men (MSM) continues to increase \[ 1 , 2 \].

HIV is mostly transmitted along various exposure networks, and the
dynamics of these networks influence the spread of the epidemic in local
populations \[ 3 , 4 \]. Recent advances in molecular epidemiology have
greatly enhanced our ability to characterize the dynamics and structure
of HIV transmission networks over space and time using HIV-1 *pol*
sequences generated for routine drug-resistance testing \[ 3 -- 6 \]. In
this study, we analyzed HIV-1 *pol* sequences generated between 2007 and
2010 from recently infected MSM in Beijing, China, to characterize an
HIV epidemic among local MSM. We then determined if inferred network
characteristics could be used to target prevention interventions such as
antiretroviral therapy (ART) efficiently.



## Abstract

***Background.*** Molecular epidemiology can be useful in identifying
clusters of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) transmission that can be
targeted for prevention.

***Methods.*** Regular screening of 2000 men who have sex with men (MSM)
in Beijing, China, for HIV infection every 2 months identified 179
primary infections (2007--2010). HIV-1 *pol* sequences were obtained and
used to infer the transmission network and identify transmitted drug
resistance (TDR) among these individuals. We evaluated the use of
clinical and network information to target prevention efforts.
Prevention efficiency was calculated as the number of infections saved
per number of interventions.

***Results.*** This cohort was infected with HIV-1 subtype B (28%),
circulating recombinant form (CRF)\_01 AE (53%), and CRF_07 BC (16%).
The overall rate of TDR was low (5%), but the rate of clustering was
high (64%), suggesting deep sampling of the subnetwork. Provision of a
theoretically high-efficacy intervention like antiretroviral therapy to
all participants had a prevention efficiency of 23%. The efficiency of
targeting prevention based on lower CD4 counts (\<200 cells/mL, \<350
cells/mL, or \<500 cells/mL) and higher viral loads (\>100 000 copies/mL
and \>50 000 copies/mL) was between 10% and 18%. The efficiency of
targeting prevention based on number of network connections was much
higher (30%--42%). For example, treating the 33 participants with ≥5
connections in 2009 would have theoretically prevented 14 infections in
2010 (42% prevention efficiency).

***Conclusions.*** Regular HIV testing of MSM in Beijing can deeply
sample the local transmission subnetwork, and targeting prevention
efforts based on network connectivity may be an efficient way to deliver
prevention interventions.

**Keywords:** HIV, molecular epidemiology, targeted prevention, China,
MSM


## METHODS

### Study Population, HIV Sequencing, and Surveillance Drug-Resistance Mutation

Study participants were HIV-1--infected individuals enrolled in a
primary infection cohort at the YouAn Hospital, Beijing, China, between
April 2007 and September 2010 (Beijing PRIMO acute HIV infection
cohort). Participants were identified with primary infection by
screening 2000 MSM for HIV infection every 2 months using enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay for antibody testing and nested polymerase chain
reaction for HIV RNA testing \[ 2 , 7 \]. All participants were
diagnosed with HIV within 2 months of their infection and had their
blood collected for CD4 T-cell count, viral load measurements, and HIV
genotyping \[ 2 , 5 , 8 \]. Sequences covered a 1.3-kb region of the
HIV-1 *pol* , including protease (amino acids 1--99) and partial reverse
transcriptase (amino acids 1--305; GenBank accession numbers
{\"type\":\"entrez-nucleotide-range\",\"attrs\":{\"text\":\"KP250654-KP250829\",\"start_term\":\"KP250654\",\"end_term\":\"KP250829\",\"start_term_id\":\"814945613\",\"end_term_id\":\"814946270\"}}
KP250654-KP250829 ). HIV-1 *pol* sequences were screened for resistance
mutations \[ 9 \]. Any surveillance drug-resistance mutation (SDRM) was
evaluated in the context of participant demographics, time period
detected, subtype, and transmission cluster.

All study participants provided informed consent for the collection of
blood samples and subsequent analyses. The study was approved by the
institution\'s ethical committee of YouAn Hospital and University of
California San Diego.

### Sequence Analysis

All HIV-1 *pol* sequences were screened for contamination, duplication,
and hypermutation using web-based tools \[ 10 \]. Sequences were
subtyped using both the subtype classification using evolutionary
algorithms program \[ 11 \] and the recombinant identification program
\[ 10 \] without disagreement between methods.

Sequence alignment and analysis was performed using HyPhy \[ 12 \], and
sequences were analyzed for genetic relatedness via pairwise distance
comparison using the Tamura-Nei 93 evolutionary model \[ 13 \]. Since
population-based sequencing often has mixed nucleotide bases, we
evaluated the following 2 clustering algorithms: leaving mixed bases
unresolved and averaging the distance between them and resolving mixed
bases for all possibilities before calculating genetic distance between
sequences. There was no substantive difference by either approach. As
previously described \[ 3 , 4 \], a putative transmission linkage was
inferred when 2 sequences had a genetic distance \<1.5% between them.
This threshold is an accepted standard for linkage based on work
demonstrating an evolutionary rate of 0.7%/year for HIV-1 *pol* within
individuals and the knowledge that the expected distance for genetically
unrelated *pol* sequences is \>5% \[ 4 , 6 , 14 \]. A cluster was then
defined as all sequences within 1.5% genetic distance from at least 1
other sequence, but not necessarily within 1.5% genetic distance of all
sequences within the cluster \[ 6 , 15 , 16 \]. Phylogenetic analysis
was performed for the circulating recombinant forms (CRFs) and subtype
predominating in China: CRF02_AE, CRF07_BC, and B. Due to its
recombinant history with subtype B, CRF07_BC was analyzed separately.
Maximum likelihood phylogenies were inferred using PHYML 3.0 \[ 17 \],
implemented in SeaView \[ 18 \] using a general time reversible model
with rate variation (GTR + Γ ~4~ ).

For the 2 largest clusters, we used BEAST (Bayesian evolutionary
analysis sampling trees) v1.8.1 \[ 19 \] to estimate the time of most
recent common ancestor (TMRCA). Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses were
run for 10 million generations under a TN93 substitution model, constant
population size, and strict molecular clock. More complicated
evolutionary models were not supported by the data. Due to the narrow
sampling window under which these sequences were obtained, a normal
prior on the substitution rate (ie, mean = 1.72 × 10--4; standard
deviation = 3 × 10--4) was used based on subtype-specific substitution
rates \[ 20 \] in addition to using date of genotyping to calibrate the
molecular clock. Sequences that did not have an associated date of
sampling were not included in this analysis. Convergence and mixing (ie,
estimated sample size for all parameters \>200) were assessed using
Tracer v1.6.

### Correlates of Clustering

For most participants, available data included demographics, HIV risk
factor, CD4 count, viral load, and HIV-1 subtype or CRF. These
characteristics were compared between individuals who clustered and
those who did not and analyzed to determine if these factors changed
over time. Categorical variables were compared using the Fisher exact
test, and continuous variables were evaluated using the Wilcoxon rank
test.

### Impact of Targeted Prevention

We determined if network or clinical data could be used to efficiently
target a prevention intervention. First, sequences that were generated
from individuals with unknown date of collection (n = 16) were excluded.
Second, we split the cohort into those diagnosed before and after 2010.
Then, we analyzed clinical and network characteristics among
participants enrolled in the cohort between 2007 and 2009 to predict the
number of infections that would have been prevented in 2010 if the
intervention had been targeted based on these characteristics. Baseline
clinical factors that were used to simulate targeting of the prevention
intervention were: CD4 counts of \<200 cells/mL, \<350 cells/mL, and
\<500 cells/mL and HIV viral loads of \>100 000 copies/mL and \>50 000
copies/mL. We also examined the efficiency of using network connectivity
to target prevention interventions by assessing the number of infections
that would have been prevented in 2010 if cohort participants had
received the intervention based on the number of connections (ie,
degrees) they had in 2009. We then considered a range of efficacy of the
prevention intervention between 30% and 100% for all individuals with
the targeted factor in each cluster by 2009. We determined the number of
clusters that were completely covered by the prevention intervention
prior to 2010 and whether an individual diagnosed in 2010 belonged to
such a cluster, then we considered that the infection would have been
prevented. We then calculated how many new infections that clustered in
2010 would have prevented based on the efficacy of the intervention. For
each clinical or network factor that was used to target interventions,
we calculated the efficiency of the prevention intervention as the
number of infections prevented per number of individuals receiving the
intervention.

## RESULTS

### Study Population

From April 2007 through September 2010, the Beijing PRIMO acute HIV
infection cohort identified 179 MSM with primary HIV infection \[ 2 \].
Demographic, CD4 count, HIV *pol* sequence, and sampling time data were
available for all of these individuals, and viral load measures were
available for 74%. The average age of participants was 32 years (range:
19--66) and 99% were of Han ethnicity. All participants were ART naive
at the time of sampling, with an average CD4 T-cell count of 464
cells/mL and viral load of 141 888 HIV RNA copies/mL. The cohort was
mostly comprised of HIV-1 subtype B (28%), CRF_01 AE (53%), and CRF_07
BC (16%) infections (Figure ​ (Figure1). 1 ). Two individuals were
infected with HIV-1 subtype C and 1 was infected with a unique
recombinant of CRF_01 AE and B. During the observation period, there was
no change in age, CD4 count, or viral loads of new participants, but
there were increased numbers of participants enrolled in 2009 (Table ​
(Table1 1 ).


### Transmitted Drug Resistance

The overall rate of SDRM in the cohort was low at 5%, which is similar
to previous reports in China \[ 21 \], and did not change appreciably
during the observation period. The most common SDRM was M46L, all among
individuals with CRF_01 AE infection. Although the M46L mutation can
decrease susceptibility to a number of protease inhibitors when present
with other mutations, it is also a natural polymorphism in CRF_01 AE \[
22 \]. There was 1 individual with subtype B infection with multiple
SDRMs including T215S, Y188L, and L90M.

### Correlates of Clustering

The inferred HIV transmission network in the cohort identified 21
clusters, involving 115/179 (64%) of the sequences, ranging from 2 to 25
individuals. Similar to previously inferred HIV-1 networks among MSM \[
3 , 23 \], the inferred transmission network was best described by a
preferential attachment model (ie, Waring distribution, *rho* = 3.19) \[
24 \]. When we examined factors associated with clustering, we found
there were no differences between individuals who clustered (n = 115)
and those who did not cluster (n = 64) based on age, CD4 count, viral
load, subtype, or SDRM (Table ​ (Table1). 1 ). We also analyzed the
number of connections each sequence had at 2010 and found no
correlations between degree and age, CD4 T-cell counts, or viral load
(data not shown).

Most of the inferred clusters were comprised of 2 individuals (ie, 41%
of clusters), but 2 clusters were large, comprising 23 and 25
individuals. One involved individuals infected with CRF_01 AE and the
other cluster contained individuals infected with CRF_07 BC. There was
no difference in mean age, CD4 T-cell counts, or viral loads of
individuals between these 2 large clusters, all of the smaller clusters,
or those individuals who did not cluster. The large CRF_01 AE cluster
was first identified in 2007 and had a peak identification of
individuals in 2009, whereas the large CRF_07 BC cluster was first noted
in 2008 and accrued individuals relatively steadily throughout the
observation period. To further evaluate the timing of these clusters, we
found that the CRF_01 AE cluster had a TMRCA in 2000 (95% highest
posterior density: 1994--2004), and the CRF_07 BC cluster had a TMRCA in
2003 (95% highest posterior density: 1998--2006).

### Targeted ART for Prevention

We next determined the number of new HIV infections diagnosed in 2010
that could have been prevented if an intervention had been targeted to
earlier cohort participants based on clinical factors measured at
enrollment (CD4 count and HIV viral load) or by number of network
connections inferred from all sequence data available in 2009. We
compared a range of efficacy (30%--100%) for our prevention intervention
and, as might be expected, found that a proportional change in
infections was prevented based on efficacy of the intervention.
Interestingly, there was little to no prevention of infections if the
prevention efficacy was \<70%. Therefore, we present here the number of
infections prevented when the efficacy of the intervention was \>75%,
which is consistent with the estimated prevention efficacy of ART \[ 25
-- 28 \]. We then considered ART for newly infected participants as the
prevention intervention throughout the rest of the analysis.

Given this, if all 134 eligible participants in 2009 were treated with
ART at baseline, we predicted that 31 infections would have been
prevented in 2010 (prevention efficiency of 23%; Figure ​ Figure2). 2 ).
The remaining 14 individuals diagnosed with recent infection in 2010 did
not cluster, so they would not have been protected by any prevention
intervention given to prior cohort participants. If ART was targeted to
cohort participants enrolled between 2007 and 2009 based on CD4 counts
of \<200 cells/mL (n = 10), \<350 cells/mL (n = 38), or \<500 cells/mL
(n = 86), then 1, 3, and 8 infections would have been prevented in 2010
(all prevention efficiencies ≤10%). Targeting ART based on viral loads
of \>100 000 copies/mL (n = 38) and \>50 000 copies/mL (n = 61) would
have prevented 4 and 11 infections in 2010 (prevention efficiencies 11%
and 18%). Therefore, targeting ART based on lower CD4 counts or higher
viral loads was less efficient than if all cohort participants were
provided ART.

Here, we show that when ART is targeted to individuals (left *y* -axis)

Next, we evaluated the number of infections that would have been
prevented in 2010 if ART had been targeted to participants enrolled
between 2007 to 2009 by number of cluster connections determined by 2009
(range: degrees ≥1 to ≥5). We found that the efficiency of ART to
prevent infections increased steadily by focusing ART on participants
who had the highest number of degrees in 2009 (Figure ​ (Figure2). 2 ).
For example, by treating the 33 participants with ≥5 connections in 2009
would have theoretically prevented 14 infections in 2010 (prevention
efficiency 42%), almost twice as high as providing ART to all
participants at the time of their diagnosis (42% vs 23%).

## DISCUSSION

This study provides 3 important insights. First, regular testing of a
local risk group such as MSM in Beijing, China, can deeply sample 1
local HIV transmission subnetwork (high rate of clustering, 62%), even
within a relatively short time (42 months). Second, HIV sequences used
for standard drug-resistance testing can be analyzed to characterize
local transmission networks; as an example, this study demonstrated a
preferential attachment model in the sampled HIV network of MSM in
Beijing. Third, targeting highly effective prevention interventions such
as ART to individuals who are highly connected in a local HIV
transmission network can be a very efficient way to prevent new
infections.

Our study cohort was constituted from a convenience sample of more than
2000 self-identified MSM living in Beijing, China, who consented to
regular HIV antibody testing every 2 months \[ 2 \]. If an individual
seroconverted, blood was collected and the HIV RNA population was
sequenced for drug-resistance testing. The prevalence of SDRM remained
relatively low and constant across the period of observation compared
with transmitted drug resistance (TDR) in the United States and Western
Europe \[ 29 \]. Even though the rate of TDR was low, it is still likely
an overestimation, since M46I/L is likely a natural polymorphism for
CRF_01AE \[ 30 \] and would not affect the current Chinese recommended
first-line regimens \[ 31 , 32 \].

The same HIV-1 *pol* sequences were then used to infer the local HIV
transmission subnetwork among these seroconverters. Even though only 179
participants were enrolled, phylogenetic analysis identified clustering
among 64% of all participants, despite a diversity of HIV-1 subtypes and
CRFs. Although somewhat higher than in other studies, this level of
clustering is consistent with deep sampling of the local network such as
other MSM cohorts \[ 3 , 5 , 33 -- 37 \], and the epidemic is relatively
new with rapid transmission. This high rate of clustering allowed us to
determine that the local network structure followed a "preferential
attachment" model, similar to other networks among MSM \[ 3 , 23 \].

Given the depth of sampling and structure of the transmission network,
we were able to determine whether prevention interventions could be
efficiently targeted to prevent future infections. Since our evaluated
prevention interventions had the largest impact on decreasing new
infections when \>75% effective, we used theoretical provision of ART as
the prevention intervention based on estimates of efficacy of ART to
prevent HIV transmission \[ 25 -- 28 \]. Since viral load is a
well-described correlate of HIV transmission \[ 26 , 38 \], we first
determined if providing individuals with high baseline HIV viral loads
with ART would be an efficient way to prevent new infections \[ 25 \].
However, targeting ART based on higher viral loads was less efficient at
preventing infections than providing ART to all participants (11% vs
23%). Interestingly, we found that prevention targeted to clustering
individuals, especially those with higher numbers of connections, was
the most efficient way of preventing new infections in the future.
Although this method seems promising, if resources are not constrained,
the best method for both the infected individual and all of their
partners is to provide ART to all infected individuals \[ 25 \].
However, the current Chinese HIV treatment guidelines only allow for
individuals with CD4 counts \<350 cells/mL to be treated \[ 31 , 32 \].
Therefore, we also evaluated CD4 count as a potential target for a
prevention intervention and found that providing ART based on low CD4
counts was not any more efficient (\<11%) than providing ART to everyone
(23%).

This study has a number of limitations, most of which concern the short,
retrospective, and observational nature of the study. These limitations
precluded us from making any definitive conclusions concerning whether
any prevention effort, including ART, targeted to highly connected
individuals is an efficient prevention intervention. For example, ART
targeted to individuals in active transmission clusters may prevent a
new individual from being infected but does not rule out the possibility
of that person getting infected from someone who was not sampled.
Further, we could have missed a number of important HIV-infected
individuals in the local network, which could greatly influence any
prevention intervention targeted on network characteristics. For
example, while recent HIV infection can account for almost half of HIV
transmissions among MSM \[ 39 \], this study ignored the contribution of
transmissions from chronically infected individuals, which is also
likely to have an important impact on epidemic spread \[ 40 \]. We could
have also falsely ascribed individuals belonging to clusters when, in
fact, they did not belong to the identified transmission network and
thus would have not been protected by any prevention measure to
individuals in that cluster. As with all prevention studies using
molecular epidemiology, the need for a rapid turnaround time on HIV
sequence generation would be important to realistically target
prevention interventions. Finally, these analyses were hampered by
missing data (eg, ongoing risk behavior, any ART use, some viral loads
at baseline, and all viral loads after baseline). In particular, some
participants could have received ART (or other effective prevention
intervention) after their HIV diagnosis that could influence clustering
over time. Since local treatment guidelines provided ART when CD4 counts
were \<350 \[ 32 \], this could explain why we observed such poor
efficiency for prevention efforts targeted based on CD4 counts \<350
cells/mL (8%). However, this would not explain why targeted efficacy
remained poor for those with CD4 counts between 350 and 500 cells/mL
(10%). Larger prospective studies should be designed to collect more
complete datasets that can address these limitations.

This study demonstrates that regular testing of a high-risk group such
as MSM in Beijing can deeply sample a local HIV transmission network and
that the analysis of HIV sequences generated from such newly diagnosed
individuals can be used to describe the underlying transmission
subnetwork. These results also demonstrate that prevention efforts based
on network data are likely more efficient than targeted interventions
based on CD4 counts or viral loads. Along these lines, "test and treat"
efforts would likely be highly efficient if based on network data.
However, we feel that universal provision of ART would likely be best
for both prevention of new infections and for the health of all infected
individuals \[ 39 , 40 \]. Until the time when universal ART is
available in China, "treatment for prevention" that is based on network
information may be useful to curb local epidemics \[ 3 \]. These same
networks may also be used to target other prevention interventions such
as improving ART adherence, providing education on safe sex, and
reducing harm.

# Treatment-emergent reverse transcriptase resistance during antiretroviral therapy with bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, and emtricitabine: A case series

Samuel DeKoven1                        |    Mark Naccarato2                    |   Chanson J. Brumme3,4                        | Darrell H. S. Tan5,6,7


Correspondence Darrell H. S. Tan, Division of Infectious Diseases, St. Michael's Hospital, 30 Bond St., Toronto, ON, Canada. Email: darrell.tan@gmail.com

Funding information Canada Research Chairs

## Abstract

Objectives:       Bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine (BIC/TAF/FTC) is a complete regimen for the treatment of HIV with a high barrier to resistance and few reported cases of treatment failure. We present three cases of treatment-emergent resistance to nucleoside/nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) in patients with suboptimal treatment adherence and assess whether the resistance-associated mutations were present before BIC/TAF/FTC initiation or emerged during therapy.

Methods: We used genotypic drug resistance testing by Sanger sequencing to identify emergent resistance mutations in plasma viral load specimens collected after combination antiretroviral therapy initiation in all participants. Additionally, we performed ultra-deep sequencing by Illumina MiSeq on the earliest available plasma HIV-1 viral load specimen and on any available specimens closest in time to the initiation of BIC/TAF/FTC therapy to identify low-abundance resistance mutations present in the viral quasispecies.

Results:      All three participants developed NRTI resistance after prolonged exposure and incomplete adherence to BIC/TAF/FTC. The T69N, K70E, M184I, and/or T215I mutations identified in clinical samples at the time of virological failure were not present on deep sequencing of either baseline samples or samples collected before BIC/TAF/FTC initiation.

Conclusions:         Despite a generally high genetic barrier to resistance, NRTI resistance-associated mutations may emerge during therapy with BIC/TAF/FTC in the setting of suboptimal adherence.

Here, we report three cases of treatment-emergent NRTI resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) to BIC/TAF/FTC, without integrase mutations.

## Case 1

A 24-year-old woman from Colombia with no relevant medical history and taking no medications was diagnosed with HIV during a routine immigration medical examination. Baseline HIV viral load was 27,699 copies/mL and CD4 count was 577 cells/μL. HIV drug-resistance genotyping using a validated in-house Sanger-sequencing assay revealed subtype B, wild-type virus [14, 15], and she was HLA-B*57:01 negative. After being lost to follow-up for 2 years, she initiated dolutegravir/abacavir/lamivudine (DTG/ABC/3TC) 39 months after diagnosis (M39); however, because of intermittent adherence, she did not experience virological suppression and was subsequently switched to BIC/TAF/FTC because of the smaller pill size while admitted to hospital with esophagitis and a CD4 count of 62 cells/μL (6%) at M59. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) was added for Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis. Repeat genotyping at M61 showed wild-type virus. She continued to be prescribed BIC/TAF/FTC with ongoing viraemia due to poor adherence. At M79, her CD4 count was 166 cells/μL (11%), viral load was 4,288 copies/mL, and genotypic resistance testing captured new reverse transcriptase (RT) mutations: T69D/N, K70E, and T215I, but she could not be contacted to switch her regimen. She discontinued BIC/TAF/FTC on her own at M82 upon learning she was pregnant. She restarted treatment with DTG + tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)/FTC at M84, before being intensified to darunavir (DRV) + ritonavir (RTV) + DTG + TDF/FTC when diagnosed with cerebral toxoplasmosis at M85. After delivery, she started DTG + rilpivirine (RPV)/TAF/FTC to reduce pill burden but did not achieve virological suppression and died of hypoxemic respiratory failure at M86.

## Case 2

A 45-year-old woman from Nigeria with no relevant medical history was diagnosed with HIV on routine screening upon immigration to Canada. Baseline viral load and CD4 count were not measured. Genotyping roughly 6 months after diagnosis (M6) showed subtype C virus and multiple protease polymorphisms with no reported decrease in drug susceptibility. She experienced an HIV RNA <40 copies/mL on initial therapy with lopinavir/RTV + zidovudine/lamivudine (AZT/3TC). She then switched to atazanavir (ATV) + RTV + TDF/FTC for simplification at M25 but reported intermittent adherence and experienced episodes of breakthrough viraemia before stopping HIV therapy at M58. Genotyping at M65 revealed the V82I protease mutation along with several genetic polymorphisms in the protease gene (Table 1). To reduce pill burden, she was switched to single-tablet efavirenz (EFV)/TDF/FTC at M66. Following several treatment interruptions, she switched to elvitegravir/cobicistat/TDF/FTC (EVG/c/TDF/FTC) at M83 and was then lost to follow-up at M96. She restarted antiretroviral therapy (ART) with EVG/c/TAF/FTC at M141 but switched to BIC/TAF/FTC due to fatigue and dizziness at M148; viral load was 128,890 copies/mL and genotype showed wild-type virus. Her other medications were TMP-SMX and a multivitamin, dosed separately from her ART. Following virological success (HIV RNA <40 copies/mL) on BIC/TAF/FTC, she experienced breakthrough viraemia (HIV RNA 18,870 copies/mL) at M161 due to poor adherence. Genotyping showed an emergent M184I mutation. She subsequently switched to BIC/TAF/FTC plus DRV/c but has yet to achieve virological success.

## Case 3

A 32-year-old man with no medical history was diagnosed with HIV in the context of a febrile illness. Baseline viral load at M2 was 283,874 copies/mL, CD4 count was 530 cells/μL, and genotyping showed wild-type subtype B virus. He initiated DRV/RTV/TDF/FTC at M5, when viral load was 2,437,253 copies/mL. He simplified the regimen to DRV/RTV alone at M9 before resuming DRV/RTV/TDF/FTC at M20 due to persistent low-level viraemia of 54–60 copies/mL between M16 and M18; viral load was <40 copies/mL at M22. At M80, viral load remained undetectable at <40 copies/mL, and at M83 he switched to BIC/TAF/FTC for simplification. Viral suppression was maintained on this regimen from M90 to M100, but he began reporting inconsistent adherence at M109, when his viral load measured 92 copies/mL. Genotyping at M112, when viral load was 2990 copies/mL, revealed a new M184I mutation. He subsequently reattained virological suppression at M126 without switching therapy.



## Materials and Methods

Resistance genotyping of baseline and follow-up specimens was performed by standard Sanger sequencing as previously described [14, 15]. Briefly, viral nucleic acids were extracted from 500 μL plasma followed by nested reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) amplification of the protease, RT, and integrase. Additionally, we performed deep sequencing using Illumina MiSeq on the earliest available viral load specimen for each patient (M7, M57, and M5, respectively) to confirm that emergent NRTI resistance mutations were not present as minority variants in the viral population before initiation of combined ART. We further tested the viral load specimens closest to the time of BIC/TAF/FTC initiation for each patient, which were from M53 and M60 (6 months before and 2 months after BIC/TAF/FTC initiation) for case 1; M148 (at time of BIC/TAF/FTC initiation) for case 2; and M109 (26 months after BIC/TAF/FTC initiation and around the time that adherence challenges emerged) for case 3. Nucleic acid extraction and RT-PCR were performed as per the Sanger sequencing protocol. MiSeq sequencing libraries were constructed from RT-PCR amplicons by Illumina Nextera XT according to manufacturer instructions and were sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq using a v2 500-cycle kit. Resulting sequence reads were analyzed by the in-house pipeline, MiCall, and low-abundance amino acid variants above 2% frequency were reported [16]. This retrospective testing was approved by the Research Ethics Board of St. Michael's Hospital, and all patients provided informed consent.

## RESULTS

For all three participants, the T69N, K70E, M184I, and/or T215I mutations reported in later samples were not detected at frequencies ≥2% with deep sequencing of the samples collected before BIC/TAF/FTC initiation. All these samples had full predicted susceptibility to all available NRTIs, non-nucleoside RT inhibitors, protease inhibitors, and integrase strand transfer inhibitors. Similarly, there was no evidence of low-abundance NRTI RAMs in the sample collected 2 months after BIC/TAF/FTC initiation in case 2, consistent with resistance emerging only after prolonged periods of suboptimal adherence to this regimen. In the sample collected 26 months after BIC/TAF/FTC initiation in case 3, there were no integrase RAMs at a frequency of >1%, but we were unable to amplify protease and RT.

## DISCUSSION

We present three patients with treatment-emergent RAMs following virological failure on BIC/TAF/FTC. All three had suboptimal adherence to BIC/TAF/FTC and developed emergent RT but not integrase resistance mutations. Case 1 developed K70E, a major resistance mutation to tenofovir, and T215I, a revertant mutation that may be present in patients with previous T215Y thymidine analog resistance mutations. Cases 2 and 3 developed M184I, a major resistance mutation selected for during failure with 3TC or FTC. The presence of a thymidine analog mutation in our first case, while never having received a thymidine-based drug, could represent archived resistance below the limit of detection of the deep-sequencing we performed, or an artefact of the RT-PCR assay. Although superinfection from repeat exposure has been reported as a cause of newly observed resistance mutations [17], phylogenetic analysis of participants' samples did not reveal substantial genetic divergence from their original virus, suggesting that superinfection was unlikely. Given the relative dearth of clinical data on BIC in pregnancy, it is also possible that pregnancy-induced changes in drug pharmacokinetics may have been a contributing factor in case 1, although this seems unlikely because she stopped BIC/TAF/FTC on her own shortly after learning she was pregnant. Finally, undisclosed concomitant use of divalent cations could also have played a causally important role in the emergence of resistance in our patients, since they would have interfered with the absorption of the BIC component of the regimen. Although BIC/TAF/FTC has a high barrier to resistance, these cases demonstrate that drug resistance can still emerge in the setting of poor adherence. Emergence of resistance has occurred both in vitro and in vivo with suboptimal drug concentrations of BIC/TAF/FTC. An in vitro study of replicating HIV exposed to varying concentrations of BIC/TAF/FTC showed multiple instances of viral breakthrough at concentrations equivalent to 4-day post-dose trough concentrations, with a single instance of emergent integrase resistance with the G163R mutation [18]. Treatment-emergent resistance with the integrase N155H mutation has also been noted with 4–5 day/week dosing of BIC/TAF/FTC, despite high levels of viral suppression overall [8, 9]. Lozano et al. reported a case of a treatment-experienced patient who developed the resistance mutations R263K and L74I in integrase and M184V in RT while receiving crushed BIC/TAF/FTC tablets through a nasogastric tube, and the authors speculated that subtherapeutic drug concentrations may have contributed [12]. Similarly, Chamberlain et al. [11] and Stoll et al. [13] observed the integrase resistance mutation R263K and RT resistance mutation M184V emerge in treatment-naïve patients receiving BIC/TAF/FTC; authors in both cases identified suboptimal adherence as a possible contributing factor. André-Garnier et al. reported one case of virological failure with the treatment-emergent integrase mutations M50I and A265V with BIC/TAF/FTC, but no mechanism for treatment failure was identified, and therapeutic drug levels suggested good adherence [10]. Finally, in a real-world cohort of patients using BIC/TAF/FTC in Spain, only one of six patients undergoing genotyping due to viral load >200 copies/mL at week 48 experienced a treatment-emergent mutation, in the form of M184V [19]. Notably, ascertainment that the original HIV isolate was wild-type in these reports was done using standard commercially available genotypic assays, which are generally unable to detect drug-resistant viruses that constitute <20% of the circulating virus population, whereas the lower limit of detection for the ultradeep sequencing assay used in our analyses was 2%.

Importantly, recent clinical trials and cohort studies demonstrated that BIC/TAF/FTC still achieved high rates of virological suppression in the presence of pre-existing NRTI RAMs [19, 20], including those that emerged in the participants described here, as illustrated by the subsequent virological suppression in case 3 despite an M184I mutation. Nevertheless, avoiding treatment-emergent resistance is important to preserve future treatment options.

A limitation of this analysis is that archived resistance mutations may not have been captured on standard genotyping, which can only detect mutations present in at least 20% of the viral population. Two of the three participants had a history of virological failure on prior regimens, such that the observed mutations may have emerged under drug pressure from those agents rather than BIC/TAF/FTC, although samples from the time of BIC/TAF/FTC initiation showed no evidence of this. Second, pre-treatment samples were not available for cases 2 and 3, although the absence of resistance mutations upon ultradeep sequencing of M2 and M26 samples after BIC/TAF/FTC initiation strongly suggests subsequent treatment-emergent resistance due to suboptimal adherence.
Similarly, we were unable to perform proviral DNA genotyping on historical samples from our patients because whole blood samples are not routinely stored;
further, given the shifting composition of the HIV reservoir over time, sequencing of proviral DNA from contemporary specimens may inadequately capture the diversity of archived proviruses. Finally, we did not measure drug concentrations to directly demonstrate
adherence, as there was sufficient clinical and virological evidence of poor adherence in all cases.
These cases demonstrate that, despite the high barrier to resistance associated with BIC/TAF/FTC, drug-resistance mutations may emerge in patients with ongoing non-adherence. Enhanced strategies for adherence support and novel medication formulations such as long-acting injectable and implantable ART may be helpful in avoiding the emergence of resistance in patients who struggle to adhere to oral medication, if the agents are fully active.

## Paper content:

# Genetic diversity of HIV-1 and transmitted drug resistance among newly diagnosed individuals with HIV infection in Hangzhou, China


## Abstract

HIV transmitted drug resistance (TDR) can compromise antiretroviral
therapy (ART) in resource-limited countries like China where ART has
been scaled up and thus leads to an important public health concern. The
aim of the study was to elucidate the HIV-1 genetic characteristics and
TDR in Hangzhou, China. Two-hundred eleven ART-naive, newly diagnosed
individuals were enrolled during January and August 2013. Specimens were
classified as recent or chronic infections using the BED capture enzyme
immunoassay (BED-CEIA). The *pol* fragment covering the entire protease
and the first 300 codons of the reverse transcriptase gene was amplified
by RT-PCR and nested PCR. Genotypic drug resistance (DR) and
phylogenetic analysis were performed on the 200 obtained sequences.
Multiple genotypes were identified, including CRF01_AE (62.0%), CRF07_BC
(31.0%), subtype B (2.0%), CRF08_BC (1.5%), CRF55_01B (1.0%), CRF18_cpx
(0.5%), and unique recombinant forms (URFs, 2.0%). All the four URFs
were found in men who have sex with men, consisting of a recombination
of CRF01_AE with subtype B or CRF07_BC. The prevalence of primary DR in
newly diagnosed individuals in Hangzhou was low (4.0%). The proportion
of DR mutation to protease inhibitors (PIs), nucleoside reverse
transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) and non-nucleoside reverse
transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) was 1.5%, 1.5%, and 1.0%,
respectively. BED-CEIA revealed that 21.8% (45/211) of the specimens
were associated with recent infections. The prevalence of TDR in recent
infections was moderate (6.5%). High HIV diversity and relatively high
prevalence of TDR in new infections has been found in Hangzhou,
indicating an increasing challenge for future HIV prevention and
treatment. ***J. Med. Virol. 87:1668--1676, 2015* .** © 2015 Wiley
Periodicals, Inc.


## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Study Patients and Sample Collection

A total of 211 newly diagnosed as HIV-positive patients were recruited
continuously between January and August 2013 in Hangzhou, Zhejiang
province. HIV-1 infection status was confirmed by Western blot assay
(HIV BLOT 2.2, MP Diagnostics, Singapore). 6--9 ml anticoagulant whole
blood with EDTA-3K as anticoagulant was collected from the study
patients. Patients\' basic demographic data were collected, including
age, gender, marital status, education status, occupation, route of
infection, etc. All patients were newly confirmed HIV-positive and
treatment naive during sampling, and had no previous exposure to HAART.
This study was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of National
Center for AIDS/STD Control and Prevention. Informed oral and written
consents were obtained from all study patients at the time of sample
collection.

### Recent Infection Detection

The BED capture enzyme immunoassay (CEIA; Calypte, Lake Oswego, OR) was
implemented in the serum with the first diagnosed as HIV-1 positive
followed the access standards. When the study patients\' CD4 lymphocytes
counts were lower than 400 cells/µl or diagnosed as AIDS in 6 months
follow-up period, the BED-CEIA results as "recent infection" were
negated.

### Amplification of HIV-1 *pol* Gene Fragments

Plasma was separated from fresh whole blood by centrifugation at 2,000
*g* for 10 min. HIV viral RNA was extracted from 140 µl of plasma by
using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according
to the manufacturer\'s protocol, and then was applied in the subsequent
reverse transcription PCR and nested PCR to generate the *pol* fragments
(HXB2: 2147-3462). The *pol* fragment covering the entire protease (PR)
and the first 300 codons of the reverse transcriptase (RT) gene was
amplified using One Step RT-PCR kit (Takara, Dalian, China) with primer
pair MAW26-07BC (5′- TGGAAATGTGGAAAAGAAGGAC -3′) / RT21-07BC (5′-
CTGTATTTCAGCTATCAAGTCTTTTGATGGG-3′) in 25 µl reaction volume. Cycling
conditions were as follows: 50°C for 30 min, 94°C for 2 min；94°C for
30 sec, 55°C for 30 sec, 72°C for 150 sec, 30 cycles；72°C for 10 min.
Nested PCR was performed using the Ex Taq DNA Polymerase (Takara,
Dalian, China) following the manufacturer\'s instructions with primer
pair PRO1-07BC (5′- CAGAGCCAACAGCCCCACCA-3′) and RT20-07BC (5′-
CTGCCAATTCTAATTCTGCTTC-3′). Cycling conditions were: 94°C for 5 min;
94°C for 30 sec, 63°C 30 sec, 72°C for 150 sec, 30 cycles; 72°C for
10 min. The PCR products were analyzed using 1% agarose gel
electrophoresis. Positive samples were sent to Beijing Zixi Bio Tech Co.
for purification and sequencing by using an ABI 3730XL automated DNA
sequencer (Applied Biosystems, Carlsbad, CA).

### Sequence Analysis

Sequence trimming and contig assembly was performed using Sequencher
v5.0 (Gene Codes, Ann Arbor, MI). The ClustalW Multiple alignment was
performed using Bio-Edit v7.2.0, followed by a few manual edits to fix
obvious misalignments. The reference sequences were retrieved from the
Los Alamos HIV sequence database ( http://www.hiv.lanl.gov ), covering
the major HIV-1 subtypes/CRFs. Phylogenetic tree analyses were
constructed using the neighbor-joining method based on Kimura
two-parameter model implemented in MEGA v6.0 \[Tamura et al., 2013 \]
with 1,000 bootstrap replicates. The potential intersubtype
recombinations were firstly analyzed using the Recombination
Identification Program (RIP) v3.0 ( http://hiv-web.lanl.gov ) \[Siepel
et al., 1995 \], and were further conducted with bootscanning and
informative site analysis using program Simplot v3.5.1 \[Lole et al.,
1999 \].

### Genotypic Analysis of HIV-1 Drug Resistance

The nucleotide sequences sets of *pol* gene in FASTA format were
submitted to the online analysis interface of Calibrated Population
Resistance (CPR) Tool v6.0 ( http://cpr.stanford.edu/cpr.cgi ) \[Gifford
et al., 2009 \] which integrated in the Stanford HIV Drug Resistance
Database ( http://hivdb.stanford.edu ). The submitted sequences with
transmitted HIV-1 drug resistance were discriminated with Genotypic
Resistance Interpretation Algorithm based on the list of Surveillance
Drug Resistance Mutations (SDRMs) recommended by WHO in 2009 \[Bennett
et al., 2009 \].

### Statistical Analyses

Statistical analyses were conducted using the Statistical Product and
Service Solutions (SPSS) v20.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY). The Person\'s χ ^2^
test or Fisher\'s exact test was applied to compare the social
demographic distribution difference. Independent-Sample *t* -test was
used to compare the difference of CD4 counts between two sections.
Statistical significance was considered when *P* values were \<0.05.

::: section

## RESULTS

### Demographic Characteristics of the Study Patients

A total of 211 eligible subjects were included in the study. The
demographics of these 211 study patients were shown in Table I . The
mean age was 33.3 (range 16--68) years old. The majority of the subjects
were male (n = 196 \[92.9%\]), single (n = 126 \[59.7%\]), of Han
ethnicity (n = 205 \[97.2%\]), had achieved compulsory education above
(n = 124 \[58.8%\]) and infected through sexual transmission (n = 209
\[99.1%\]). The mean CD4 counts of the study patients when sampled were
436.2 cells/µl (SD, 227.0). 53.6% of subjects permanently resided in
Zhejiang province, while 46.4% had household registration in other
provinces.

According to the results of the BED-CEIA, 46 specimens (21.8%) were
classified as recent HIV-1 infection (section 1) and 165 specimens
(78.2%) were classified as being associated with chronic HIV-1 infection
(section 2). There was no significant statistical difference between
section 1 and section 2 in social demographic distribution, except for
age, education status and CD4 cell counts. Section 1 showed being
younger, higher proportion of compulsory education above and higher
immune status when compared to that of section 2.

### HIV-1 Subtypes and Phylogenetic Analysis

The partial gene of HIV-1 *pol* (1316 bp, encoding the entire PR and
first 300 RT gene region) was amplified. 11 of 211 samples failed to
amplify, while 200 (94.8%) were successfully amplified, sequenced, and
included in the phylogenetic analysis (Fig. 1 ). CRF01_AE was the
dominant subtype (62.0%, 124/200), followed by CRF07_BC (31.0%, 62/200),
subtype B (2.0%, 4/200), CRF08_BC (1.5%, 3/200), CRF55_01B (1.0%,
2/200), CRF18_cpx (0.5%, 1/200), and URFs (2.0%, 4/200). Novel CRFs such
as CRF18_cpx (HZ131344) and CRF55_01B (HZ130990 and HZ130991) were first
discovered in the area in this study (Table II ). There were four
sequences that did not match known CRFs, and thus were classified as
URFs (2.0%), of which two cases (HZ130207 and HZ130743) were determined
as CRF01_AE/B, the remaining two cases (HZ130198 and HZ130947) as
CRF01_AE/CRF07_BC (Fig. 2 ). All the four cases were infected through
homosexual contact. Isolate HZ130207 displayed a recombination structure
with subtype B and CRF01_AE determined at positions 2253-2527 and
2528-3460, respectively. Isolate HZ130743 displayed a mosaic
recombination pattern with CRF01_AE segments identified at positions
2253-2995 and subtype B segments at positions 2996-3448. Isolate
HZ130198 showed a recombination genomic structure, with CRF07_BC
segments identified at positions 2253-2956 and CRF01_AE segments at
positions 2957-3414. Isolate HZ130947 displayed a mosaic recombination
pattern with 2253-2593 nt originated from CRF01_AE while 2594-3455 nt
from CRF07_BC.

### Transmitted Drug Resistance

TDR mutations were identified by CPR tool through the Stanford HIV Drug
Resistance Database. Of the 200 samples that amplified successfully,
eight were found to have primary resistance mutations (Table III ),
representing an overall primary DR prevalence of 4.0% (8/200). More
specifically, the proportions of DR mutation to protease inhibitors
(PIs), nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs), and
non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) were 1.5%
(3/200), 1.5% (3/200), and 1.0% (2/200), respectively. All the patients
with DR harbored only one resistance mutation, and infected with
CRF01_AE strains by sexual contact (Table III ). Among PI-related DR
mutations, the major mutation M46I, which decreases susceptibility to
nelfinavir (NFV), was found in two patients. G73S was detected in
another patient. Among NRTI-related DR mutations, M184V that causes
high-level resistance to Lamivudine (3TC) and Emtricitabine (FTC) was
found in two patients. K70E was found in one patient. Among
NNRTI-related DR mutations, V106M and G190A that cause high-level
resistance to Neviapine (NVP) were each found in one patient. Three
cases of the patients with DR were classified as recent infection, while
the others were classified as being associated with chronic infection.

**Prevalence Categories of TDR**

According to categories recommended by WHO, the prevalence of primary DR
in ART-naive population was low (\<5.0%). According to the results of
the BED-CEIA, 46 specimens (21.8%) were classified as recent HIV-1
infection and 165 specimens (78.2%) were classified as being associated
with chronic HIV-1 infection. Drug resistance was identified among 6.5%
(3/46) of specimens classified as recent infection and 3.0% (5/165) of
specimens classified as chronic infection. Therefore, the prevalence of
TDR in the recent infections was moderate (5--15%).

::: section

## DISCUSSION

The prevalence of TDR has important implications for the successful
management of HAART among infected individuals as it restricts ART
choices and increases the risk of treatment failure. The surveillance of
TDR in China has particularly important public health significance owing
to the limited resources of antiretroviral drugs. This is a systematic
study that describes HIV-1 genetic diversity and the prevalence of TDR
among newly diagnosed individuals with HIV infection in Hangzhou after
the start of the ART program. We found that the overall prevalence of
primary DR was 4.0%. This prevalence was comparable to that of previous
studies in China, which showed 3.8% TDR in China during 2004 and 2005
\[Liao et al., 2010 \], 3.2% in Guangxi in 2013 \[Li et al., 2014 \],
2.7% in Taizhou prefecture during 2008--2011 \[Hua et al., 2015 \], 4.9%
among MSM in 19 provinces/cities in 2010 \[Yang et al., 2013 \]. The
prevalence of DR in our study which categorized as low level was similar
to Southern Vietnam \[Tanuma et al., 2014 \] and Malaysia \[Ong et al.,
2014 \] on the whole, but lower than those in North America and Western
Europe where TDR rates were reported to be 13.6% and 6.8% during 2004 to
2006 \[Rahim et al., 2009 \], respectively. The result was
understandable, as China, like other Asian countries, has had a shorter
period of access to HAART than in developed countries.

It is obvious that TDR survey based on the newly diagnosed individuals
may include patients with chronic HIV infection, which may have an
opportunity for reversion of mutant variants to wild-type stains or to
reduce to an undetectable level by PCR. This may result in
underestimating the true prevalence of TDR in the population. BED-CEIA
can classify the types of HIV-1 infection (recent versus chronic), thus
can be applied in the population-based prevalence of TDR in the recently
infected individuals \[Parekh et al., 2002 ; Jayaraman et al., 2006 ;
Murillo et al., 2010 \]. Though BED-CEIA exhibits a certain rate of
false-recent misclassification \[Moyo et al., 2014 \], it still has
higher predictive value of recent infection than indiscriminate sampling
or sampling with younger age alone \[Murillo et al., 2010 \]. In this
study, we made further exclusion on the basis of CD4 counts and clinic
diagnosis, which could be predicted to reduce false positive cases.
Based on the BED-CEIA data, 21.8% of the specimens were associated with
recent infections, while 78.2% probably chronic HIV infection. The TDR
prevalence in recent infected population was 6.5%, a little higher than
that in the total population (4.0%). The present study confirms previous
findings that relatively higher prevalence of TDR among recent
infections \[Jayaraman et al., 2006 ; Yanik et al., 2012 \]. The
prevalence of TDR based on recent infected populations gave more
enlightenment for the latest prevalence of DR, portending the trends for
the future. There is more enlightening information from the BED-CEIA
data. We found a low proportion of specimens classified as recent
infections as determined by BED-CEIA, which indicates late HIV diagnosis
is common in Hangzhou, suggesting great efforts should be made to
increase access to HIV testing. Recent HIV infection happened more among
young people with higher educational level should be given more
attention.

The first-line ART regimens in China consist of two kinds of NRTIs
combined with one kind of NNRTI, while the second-line regimens contain
PI together with NRTIs and NNRTIs. Previous studies reported relatively
high rates of TDR mutations to PIs in ART-naive patients especially
among MSM \[Zhao et al., 2011 ; Yang et al., 2013 \]. It was estimated
that the majority of PI-DR strains were derived from foreign countries
with prolonged ART history. However, the RTI SDRMs (five cases) were
more than PI SDRMs (three cases) in this study. A summary report of ART
in Zhejiang province in 2013 showed that 85.4% used the first-line ART
regimens, while 14.6% used the second-line regimens (data unpublished).
The mutations M46I, M184V, and G190A that covered five cases in this
study were listed in the top five of DR mutations sorting by frequency
in patients with virological failure in the whole province. The higher
prevalence of RTI mutations as compared to PI mutations is probably due
to a broader and longer use of these drugs in Hangzhou. This indicated
that DR strains were probably from the domestic transmission,
highlighting the importance of timely and effective intervention
measures for TDR. Furthermore, early initiation of ART had piloted as a
prevention strategy among MSM in Hangzhou in very recent years. Our
study revealed the characteristics of TDR in this region, which is
essential and timely for implement and evaluation of the preventive
measure as well.

The increasing HIV diversity has profound implications for many aspects
of the pandemic, including viral pathogenicity, transmission, diagnosis,
treatment, and vaccine development \[Aldrich and Hemelaar, 2012 \].
Though the sequences of *pol* segment give limited information on
recombination, it can still provide important information about HIV
diversity in the study area where such information is scarce. The
present study provided a latest update on the molecular diversity of
HIV-1 among the newly diagnosed HIV-infected patients in Hangzhou.
Phylogenetic analysis revealed that CRF01_AE remained as the major
circulating recombinant form especially among patients infected through
sexual contact, consistent with previous studies in Zhejiang province
\[Zhang et al., 2013 \]. It is notable that the complexity and diversity
of HIV strains seems to increase. Novel HIV subtypes including CRF18_cpx
(one case) and CRF55_01B (two cases) were first discovered and reported
in the area. Furthermore, four URFs consisting of a recombination of
CRF01_AE with subtype B or CRF07_BC were identified in the study. It is
worth noting that the novel subtypes and URFs were mainly found in MSM.
CRF55_01B among MSM in China was firstly identified in 2012 \[Han et
al., 2013 \], and recently reported a outbreak among MSM in Shenzhen
with 9.2% (99/1072) in all subtyped sequences \[Zhao et al., 2014 \].
The sporadic detection of CRF55_01B in Hangzhou might be a prelude of
outbreak among MSM in the near future. It is worth closely tracking and
monitoring. It was reported higher rates of dual-variant and
multiple-variant HIV infection in MSM than in heterosexual people in the
same populations \[Li et al., 2010 ; Beyrer et al., 2012 \], which
increased the chances of HIV recombination. There is growing concern
that URFs can be prone to formation due to MSM\'s special behavior
feature with multiple sex partners and low rate of condom use. The
existence of four URFs in this study let the worry into reality and
reveals the fact that new viruses have generated and may be prevalent
among the population. However, given the status that there were B,
CRF01_AE and CRF07_BC co-circulating in MSM in China \[Wang et al., 2008
; Zhao et al., 2011 ; Wang et al., 2012 \], it was not surprising that
HIV-1 URFs generated through recombination between CRF01_AE and subtype
B or CRF07_BC among the MSM. Additionally, there was a cause for concern
that almost all novel CRFs and URFs in this study were found in the
patients with local residence and chronic infection defined by BED-CEIA,
hinting the profound dynamic change of HIV complexity in the near
future. The increasing HIV diversity poses important challenges for the
HIV prevention and treatment efforts. Thus, further research will be
needed to elucidate the mechanism of HIV-1 molecular evolution and
recombination.

The limitation of this study is that it included only one representative
region in Zhejiang province. More effort is needed to expand across
province to acquire comprehensive monitoring and surveillance of TDR.
Our laboratory-based study provided some clues in the characteristics of
HIV-1 epidemic. However, the lack of follow-up epidemiological survey
makes source tracking unachievable.

In conclusion, our study indicates that the prevalence of DR in
ART-naive population and recent infected population were low and
moderate, respectively, and the HIV-1 epidemic in the area was
characterized by multiple subtypes and recombinant forms. The findings
in this study may help to guide recommendations for diagnostic assays,
vaccine design and ART strategies in China.

# Transmitted drug resistance in recently infected HIV-positive Individuals from four urban locations across Asia (2007--2010) -- TASER-S


## Abstract

### Background

The availability of HIV antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been associated
with the development of transmitted drug resistance-associated mutations
(TDRM). TDRM can compromise treatment effectiveness in patients
initiating ART and the prevalence can vary in different clinical
settings. In this study, we investigated the proportion of TDRM in
treatment-naïve, recently infected HIV-positive individuals sampled from
four urban locations across Asia between 2007--2010.

### Methods

Patients enrolled in the TREAT Asia Studies to Evaluate Resistance --
Surveillance Study (TASER-S) were genotyped prior to ART initiation,
with resulting resistance mutations analysed according to the WHO 2009
list.

### Results

Proportions of TDRM from recently infected individuals from TASER-S
ranged from 0% to 8.7% - Hong Kong: 3/88 (3.4%, 95% CI (0.71%-9.64%));
Thailand: Bangkok: 13/277 (4.7%, 95% CI (2.5%-7.9%)), Chiang Mai: 0/17
(0%, 97.5% CI (0%-19.5%)); and the Philippines: 6/69 (8.7%, 95% CI
(3.3%-18.0%)). There was no significant increase in TDRM over time
across all four clinical settings.

### Conclusions

The observed proportion of TDRM in TASER-S patients from Hong Kong,
Thailand and the Philippines was low to moderate during the study
period. Regular monitoring of TDRM should be encouraged, especially with
the scale-up of ART at higher CD4 levels.

**Keywords:** Transmitted, Drug resistance, Asia, Resource-limited,
Recent-infection

## Methods

Treatment-naïve, recently HIV-infected patients were recruited into the
TREAT Asia Studies to Evaluate Resistance -- Surveillance Study
(TASER-S) between 2007-2010 \[ 7 \] from 5 participating sites: 2 from
Hong Kong SAR, China; 1 from Bangkok, Thailand; 1 from Chiang Mai,
Thailand; and 1 from Manila, Philippines. Patients were included in
TASER-S according to the following inclusion criteria:

***Hong Kong SAR, China:*** patients were selected from those who
attended the two participating clinics and satisfied one of these
criteria: (a) age up to 25 years old; (b) negative HIV test within one
year; or (c) BED assay positive.

***Bangkok, Thailand:*** patients were enrolled from a voluntary
counselling and testing centre in Bangkok. All modes of HIV exposure
were considered, however male patients with homosexual HIV exposure were
selectively chosen to be enrolled in 2010. Recent HIV infection was
defined as a new HIV diagnosis in subjects \<25 years old. For those who
were older, previous HIV-negative documentation within the past
12 months was required for study inclusion.

***Chiang Mai, Thailand:*** patients presented to care at the
participating hospital were selected for enrolment. Patients were
included if they had a confirmed HIV-positive test and were aged
\<25 years with no prior AIDS-defining illnesses.

***Manila, Philippines:*** blood samples were obtained from the STD AIDS
Cooperative Central Laboratory, the National Reference Laboratory for
HIV and Other STIs (NRL-SACCL). All samples obtained from asymptomatic
patients were tested using the BED assay. Those with positive BED tests
were presumed to be recently infected and included in TASER-S.

CD4 count was not used as a criteria in TASER-S as the study protocol
was developed prior to the WHO 2008 surveillance recommendations \[ 8
\], and it was not known a priori the time lag for obtaining CD4
results.

Genotyping was performed at TREAT Asia Quality Assessment Scheme (TAQAS)
certified laboratories \[ 9 \]. Pre-treatment *pol* gene FASTA files
were submitted to the Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database
\[ 10 \] Version 6.2 for genotyping and REGA HIV-1 Subtyping Tool \[ 11
, 12 \] - Version 2.0 for subtyping. RAMs were analysed according to the
WHO 2009 list \[ 13 \]. TDRM was defined as having ≥1 RAM. Patients with
both protease (PR) and reverse transcriptase (RT) sequences available
were included.

Clinical characteristics, including age, sex, mode of HIV exposure,
viral load, CD4 count and HIV-1 subtype, were reported descriptively.
Time trends were analysed using chi-squared test for trend. Confidence
intervals (CI) for proportion of RAMs were calculated using the exact
binomial methods. A sensitivity analysis was performed by including
patients who were missing a PR or RT sequence file by assuming an
absence of RAMs in the missing gene region and also by including those
with extensive RAMs without confirmation of their treatment naïve
status. All data management and statistical analyses were performed
using SAS software version 9.3 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) and
STATA software version 12.1 (STATA Corp., College Station, TX, USA).

Data transfers were aggregated at The Kirby Institute, UNSW Australia.
Ethics approvals were obtained from UNSW Australia Ethics Committee and
institutional review boards at the participating clinical sites and
coordinating centre (TREAT Asia/amfAR, Bangkok, Thailand). Written
informed consent was obtained from participants prior to enrolment --
except in the Philippines, where anonymous samples were obtained from
the NRL-SACCL and consent was waived.

## Results

### Hong Kong SAR, China

A total of 88 patients were included from the 2 sites (Table 1 ). The
overall proportion was 3/88 (3.4%, 95% CI (0.71%-9.64%)). Figure 1 shows
TDRM in 2007 was 0/28 (0.0%); 2008: 2/32 (6.3%); 2009: 1/21 (4.8%); and
2010: 0/7 (0.0%), p-trend = 0.631.



Table 2 shows a list of RAMs harboured by different individuals. Of the
3 patients with RAMs from Hong Kong, 1 patient had a PR RAM (M46I) and 2
patients had one RT RAM each (K103N and M41L).


### Bangkok, Thailand

Recruitment occurred between 2008--2010 with a total of 277 patients.
TDRM was present in 13/277 (4.7%, 95% CI (2.5%-7.9%)). The proportions
of TDRM by year were: 2008: 4/118 (3.4%); 2009: 4/83 (4.8%); and 2010:
5/76 (6.6%), p-trend = 0.305 (Figure 1 ). The most common PR-RAM was
M46I (6 patients) and the most common RT-RAM was Y181C (3 patients)
(Table 2 ).

### Chiang Mai, Thailand

Seventeen patients were enrolled into the study during the years 2007 (4
patients), 2008 (10 patients) and 2009 (3 patients). No patient
harboured RAMs, with 97.5% one-sided CI of (0%-19.5%).

### Manila, Philippines

Blood samples were collected from 69 patients. TDRM was present in 6/69
patients (8.7%, 95% CI (3.3%-18.0%)). Figure 1 shows in 2008, 0/1
patients (0.0%) had TDRM; 2009: 6/67 (9.0%); and 2010: 0/1 (0.0%),
p-trend \>0.999.

Out of the 6 patients who harboured RAMs, all but one harboured only one
resistance mutation (Table 2 ).

### Sensitivity analysis

With the inclusion of 5 patients with missing RT region and 3 patients
with extensive mutations from Bangkok, the total proportion of TDRM for
this site increased to 5.6% with 95% CI (3.2%-9.0%). The yearly trend of
TDRM was not significant at p = 0.256. For Manila, the inclusion of 13
patients with missing PR or RT sequences increased the proportion to
7/82 (8.5%, 95% CI (3.5%-16.8%)), p-trend = 0.860.

## Discussion

Observed proportions of TDRM in this study ranged from 0% to 8.7%, with
no significant increase in trend over time. TASER-S participants were
predominantly men who have sex with men (MSM). Studies have shown that
MSM was associated with the presence of TDRM with higher rates of
resistance reported in this group \[ 5 , 14 \]. Although each TASER-S
site utilised a different recruitment strategy which prevents direct
comparison of TDRM across sites, the findings of this study suggests
that the Philippines, a country that has not yet encountered a national
epidemic comparable to other Southeast Asian countries \[ 15 \], had a
relatively higher TDRM proportion of 8.7%. This could be due to other
non-B subtypes \[ 16 \] prevalent in the sample (26.1%) and may warrant
further investigation into the extent of HIV RAMs within the country and
the associated key population at risk.

The proportion of TDRM for Hong Kong (3.4%) and Bangkok (4.7%) were
similar to that found previously \[ 5 , 17 \] although there were
differences in the sample sizes and sampling methodology. Chiang Mai
reported 0% TDRM, but given that only 17 patients were enrolled, it is
not possible to exclude drug resistance prevalence as high as 19.5%.

Our study had several limitations including the potential sampling bias
within the study. TASER-S included only patients attending TREAT Asia
sites. Informed consent was required from all participants, except in
the Philippines, and this may further contribute to sampling bias by
allowing only those who consented to be included in the study. Other
limitations were the possibility of patients experiencing reversion of
RAMs back to wild-type \[ 18 , 19 \]; and the possibility of
misclassification by BED assay due to its high false recent rates \[ 20
\], although this only applies to patients recruited from Hong Kong and
the Philippines. Findings of TDRM reported in this study only reflect
those participating in TASER-S and may not be generalisable to the
broader HIV-infected population across the region.

Go to:


## Conclusions

In summary, the observed proportion of TDRM in TASER-S patients from
Hong Kong, Thailand and the Philippines was low to moderate during the
study period. With the 2013 WHO guidelines recommending ART initiation
in persons with CD4 count ≤500 cells/μL \[ 21 \], and the possible
scale-up of ART due to "Test and Treat" strategies \[ 22 \], further
monitoring of acquired drug resistance in individuals on ART, as well as
regular surveillance of recently infected persons should be encouraged.
